extracted.intended_audience: writers, literature students, and general readers interested in narrative techniques
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what a frame story is, how and why to use framing devices (nesting, false documents, dream visions, unreliable narrators, reprise, etc.) and examples of their effects in literature and other media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — frame story / frame narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: A literary technique (also called frame tale, framing device, sandwich narrative, or intercalation) where an introductory or main narrative sets the stage either for a more emphasized second narrative or for a set of shorter stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads readers from a first story into one or more other stories within it; may inform readers about aspects of the secondary narrative(s) that would otherwise be hard to understand. Examples: One Thousand and One Nights, The Decameron. Note: should not be confused with narrative structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary function — must act as occasion for other stories
rubrics_metrics.description: To be a frame narrative, the story must act primarily as an occasion for the telling of other stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Odysseus narrating to the Phaeacians — the framed tales are principally occasions for the embedded narratives, not merely background recollection. Distinguish true frame narratives from works where interpolated recollections are subordinate to the main plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizing conceit / collection device (mise en abyme)
rubrics_metrics.description: A frame story acts as a convenient conceit to organize a set of smaller narratives, either devised by the author or adapted from existing tales; sometimes a story within the main narrative encapsulates some aspect of the framing story (mise en abyme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when you want to assemble varied tales under a single unifying device. Examples include Scheherazade in One Thousand and One Nights and Ovid's Metamorphoses. Can incorporate previously existing material slightly altered for the longer narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nested / Chinese-box narrative (multiple layers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frames can be nested several deep, creating stories within stories within stories (a 'Chinese box' narrative), allowing inclusion of many different tales in one work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful for anthologies or works that benefit from multiple levels of perspective. Examples: Ovid, The Sandman 'Worlds End' arc, and the nested tales in One Thousand and One Nights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting doubt on the narrator / unreliable narrator framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly making the narrator a character within the frame distances the writer from that narrator and may be used to cast doubt on the narrator's truthfulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterize the frame narrator (their vocation, personality) to create skepticism in the reader. Examples: P. G. Wodehouse's Mr. Mulliner (a teller of tall tales), the framing of Amadeus as Salieri's stories—used to signal unreliability or bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procatalepsis — position readers' reactions to engage interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a frame where characters listening to a tale voice potential reader reactions (procatalepsis) so the story can anticipate or defuse those reactions and thereby engage interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when the main tale lacks a strong narrative hook; the frame's listeners can express cynicism or curiosity that the audience might feel. Example: The Princess Bride's grandfather/grandson frame that channels a viewer's possible reaction to a romantic fairytale; also used in Edith Wharton's Ethan Frome.

rubrics_metrics.name: False documents as a framing device
rubrics_metrics.description: A frame story may use 'false documents' (letters, transcripts, notes) to explain how the story-within-a-story was discovered or recorded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This device can create a sense of authenticity or archival discovery. Examples: letters in Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, the 'Historical Notes' epilogue of The Handmaid's Tale, and epistolary novels in general.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dream vision framing
rubrics_metrics.description: A specialized frame where the narrator claims to have dreamed the events of the tale and then tells the dream, historically used to indicate fictionality or divine revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in medieval literature (Chaucer) and used to manage readers' suspension of disbelief; John Bunyan used it to present allegory as divinely inspired dreams. Can be used in fantasy for a protective frame, but may also undercut the reality of the tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictitious author persona as frame
rubrics_metrics.description: The conceit that the author of the book is not the real author but a fictional character who 'presents' or 'collected' the tales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This layer can create distance and an assumed readership that 'plays along' with the conceit. Example: Washington Irving's use of the fictional Crayon as the book's presented author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reprise / recurrent-element framing
rubrics_metrics.description: A framing device can take the form of a recurrent element at the beginning and end (reprise), or return periodically to convey a defining emotion or tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a repeated scene, image, or motif at the work's start and finish to provide context and show change. Example: Chariots of Fire begins and ends with the characters running along a beach, using the scene to convey tone and emotional continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium and genre flexibility — film, comics, novels, epistolary forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame stories appear across media (novels, films, comics, song cycles) and genres; the device can be adapted to suit medium-specific needs (e.g., voiceover narration in film, epistolary documents in novels, story arcs in comics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how medium affects the frame's affordances: cinematic frames may use voiceover or flashback sequences (Forrest Gump, Slumdog Millionaire); comics may structure arcs as framed tales (The Sandman). Choose framing techniques that align with medium-specific storytelling tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect on verisimilitude and reader attitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Frames can be used either to increase suspension of disbelief (e.g., dream frames used in fantasy) or to cast doubt on the truth of events (e.g., dream frames that indicate fictionality or unreliable narrators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your frame should bolster the reader's belief in the tale (present as discovered documents, eyewitness accounts) or encourage skepticism (obvious fictional narrator, dream framing). Examples: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz film's dream frame detracts from the fantasy's validity; dream frames in medieval allegory can make events more acceptable as revelation.
